query: For high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what testable methodological hypothesis could enable improved combinations of strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance? Explain why it should work, what measurable improvement is expected relative to the state of the art, the conditions under which it should or should not hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an experimental result that would decisively falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing controlled short-range order (SRO) through a dual-stage annealing treatment will improve the balance of strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance in a single‐phase FCC high-entropy alloy relative to a conventional homogenized (disordered) state.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic FCC high-entropy alloy (for example, CrCoNi) produced by hot rolling that yields a largely homogeneous, disordered solid-solution microstructure.
generation.intervention: Apply a dual-stage annealing process: first, a high-temperature homogenization step to remove segregation; then a carefully controlled medium-duration, lower-temperature annealing step designed to promote the formation of nanoscale short-range order (SRO) without precipitating secondary phases.
generation.conditions: The high-entropy alloy (e.g., CrCoNi) is processed identically up to hot rolling. The intervention uses precise annealing parameters (temperature T2 and time) determined by preliminary atom probe tomography studies to reach the threshold for inducing SRO while retaining the FCC phase. Mechanical testing (tensile, compression, fracture toughness tests) is performed at room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale SRO clusters within the FCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: The formation of SRO clusters is expected to locally impede dislocation motion, thus promoting a work‐hardening effect that simultaneously increases yield strength and fracture resistance. At the same time, because SRO is not associated with coarse precipitate formation or catastrophic phase decomposition, the intrinsic ductility and the elastic stiffness (Young’s modulus) remain high.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline (a homogenized, hot-rolled alloy without the SRO-inducing second-stage), the dual-stage annealed alloy should exhibit a measurable increase in yield strength and fracture toughness (improvements that might be on the order of a noticeable percentage increase though the exact magnitude is to be established) while maintaining or modestly increasing ductility and Young’s modulus.
generation.baseline: The same FCC high-entropy alloy in its conventional hot-rolled/homogenized (disordered) state without the additional SRO-inducing annealing step.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable only in alloys that form a single-phase FCC solid solution and that possess an intrinsic tendency toward forming SRO under controlled thermal exposure. It may not hold if the second-stage annealing parameters lead to unwanted precipitate formation or grain coarsening, or in HEAs that do not develop appreciable SRO.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal annealing temperature/time window for inducing beneficial SRO and the precise magnitude of improvements in mechanical properties require further experimental optimization and may vary with alloy composition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of the target equiatomic FCC HEA. Process both identically up to the hot rolling/homogenization step. Then, subject one set to the dual-stage annealing (with the second stage optimized to induce SRO) and leave the control set without this additional SRO-inducing step. Characterize the microstructure using atom probe tomography and transmission electron microscopy to confirm the presence (or absence) of nanoscale SRO. Finally, perform identical tensile, compression, and fracture toughness tests at room temperature on both sets.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the SRO-induced samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in yield strength and fracture toughness (while maintaining comparable ductility and Young’s modulus) relative to the control samples, then the hypothesis is refuted.

cited_evidence.text: Medium- and high-entropy alloys are an emerging class of materials that can exhibit outstanding combinations of strength and ductility for engineering applications. Computational simulations have suggested the presence of short-range order (SRO) in these alloys, and recent experimental evidence is also beginning to emerge. Unfortunately, the difficulty in quantifying the SRO under different heat treatment conditions has generated much debate on the atomic preferencing and implications of SRO on mechanical properties. Here we develop an approach to measure SRO using atom probe tomography. This method balances the limitations of atom probe tomography with the threshold values of SRO to map the regimes where the required atomistic neighbourhood information is preserved and where it is not. We demonstrate the method with a case study of the CoCrNi alloy and use this to monitor SRO changes induced by heat treatments. These species-specific SRO measurements enable the generation of computational simulations of atomic neighbourhood models that are equivalent to the experiment and can contribute to the further understanding and design of medium- and high-entropy alloys and other materials

As a class of advanced metal materials, high/medium-entropy alloys (H/MEAs) hold great promise for overcoming the property bottleneck in conventional alloys [,]. Among many studies [,,], an equiatomic CrCoNi MEA with a face-centered cubic (FCC) structure has emerged as one of the most damage-tolerant alloys to date. Despite its excellent ductility, the alloy always showed a lower yield strength of approximately 350 MPa, because of the multiple slip systems, similar to other FCC alloys []. This severely limits its engineering serviceability for structural applications. Exploring appropriate strategies to overcome the strength–ductility trade-off has been a major objective for the CrCoNi MEA [].
